work.text: To Daumier the brutal soldiery of 1834 had been evil for their brutality rather than for the cause they served. He was a humanitarian too sincere to condone a cruelty because committed by his party’s friends.

source.author: Michael Sadleir
source.title: Daumier: The Man and the Artist

moment.text: During the uprising, sniper fire directed toward government troops emanated from a house on the Rue Transnonain. In retaliation, the soldiers indiscriminately massacred residents, including old men, women, and children.
Between 1830 and 1835 censorship laws had been suspended, allowing Charles Philipon (1806–1862) to publish a number of periodicals like L'Association Mensuelle, where Rue Transnonain appeared.

matters.text: Daumier has chosen the moment following the massacre. A deadly silence seems to pervade the place depicted. … The horror of such material is obviated for us only by the serene nobility of the method.

source.author: Elisabeth Luther Cary
source.title: Honoré Daumier: A Collection of His Social and Political Caricatures, with an Introductory Essay on His Art

matters.text: In this haunting image, Daumier focused attention on the human suffering and loss of life, emphasizing the innocence of the victims and the violence of their deaths.
